units.name: Cash flow and the balance sheet

terms.short: How fast sales are rising
terms.definition: The percentage change in a company's sales against an earlier period, usually the same quarter last year. It is the first number traders check in results, because profits can't grow for long without it. Growth from price rises and from volumes mean different things.
examples: Revenue growth of 18% beat the street's 12%, and the stock opened 5% higher.
Revenue growth slowed to 4%, and margins can't carry the story forever.
Half the revenue growth came from price hikes, not more volume.
terms.fill: Sales up 15% on the same quarter last year is the company's ____.
wrong: Profit as a share of sales
Cash left after capex
Profit growth after tax

reads.up: Faster revenue growth, especially above estimates, usually lifts the stock and can lead analysts to raise targets; check that it comes from volume, not one-offs.
reads.down: Slowing revenue growth worries the market even if profit beats, because it says future earnings will grow slower; high-multiple stocks fall hardest.

terms.short: Profit before interest, tax and D&A, over sales
terms.definition: EBITDA divided by revenue: how many paise of operating profit, before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, a company keeps from each rupee of sales. It shows pricing power and cost control, and is compared across quarters and with peers in the same industry.
examples: EBITDA margin expanded 200 bps as raw material costs fell.
Revenue beat, but the EBITDA margin missed by 150 bps, so the stock fell.
Cement makers' EBITDA margins swing with fuel prices.
terms.fill: EBITDA of ₹200 crore on sales of ₹1,000 crore is a 20% ____.
wrong: Net profit divided by equity
Sales growth over a year
The share of profit paid as dividend

calcs.q: Sales are ₹2,500 crore and EBITDA is ₹450 crore. What is the EBITDA margin?

reads.up: Margin expansion means the company is pricing well or cutting costs; it often drives earnings upgrades and a re-rating.
reads.down: Margin contraction signals cost pressure or weaker pricing power; the market usually punishes it, even with good sales.

terms.short: Profit after tax: the bottom line
terms.definition: Profit after tax: what's left for shareholders after all costs, interest, depreciation and tax. Indian results headlines usually lead with it. Divide by shares outstanding to get EPS. It can be moved by one-offs, so check what drove it.
examples: PAT rose 25%, but a tax write-back did most of the work.
Street estimate for PAT was ₹1,200 crore; it came in at ₹1,310 crore.
Strong PAT growth with weak revenue usually means something one-off.
terms.fill: Profit left for shareholders after all costs and tax is the ____.
wrong: Sales before any costs
Profit before interest and tax
Cash from operations

reads.up: PAT beating estimates usually lifts the stock, but check the quality: tax gains or other income don't count as much as operating profit.
reads.down: A PAT miss usually drags the stock, unless it comes from a one-off charge the market looks through.

terms.short: Compared with the same period last year
terms.definition: Growth measured against the same quarter or month a year earlier. It removes seasonal swings, such as festive-season sales, which is why Indian results are mostly judged on it. A weak base last year can flatter the number.
examples: Year-on-year growth of 40% looks great, but last year's quarter was hit by a strike.
Auto sales are compared year-on-year because October and November carry the festive season.
On a low base, year-on-year growth is easy.
terms.fill: Comparing this October's sales with last October's to avoid seasonal effects is measuring ____.
wrong: Comparing with the previous quarter
The average growth over five years
Comparing with the industry average

terms.short: Compared with the previous quarter
terms.definition: Growth measured against the quarter just before. It shows the latest direction faster than year-on-year, but seasonal businesses can swing a lot between quarters, so read it alongside year-on-year growth.
examples: Sales rose against the June quarter for the first time in a year: quarter-on-quarter growth has turned positive.
IT services firms are judged on quarter-on-quarter dollar revenue growth.
Don't panic on a quarter-on-quarter drop for a retailer: Q4 always follows the festive quarter.
terms.fill: Comparing July–September sales with April–June sales is measuring ____.
wrong: Comparing with the same quarter last year
Growth over the full financial year
Growth in share price over a quarter

terms.short: Fixed costs make profit swing more than sales
terms.definition: When a big share of costs is fixed, a rise in sales lifts profit by much more in percentage terms, and a fall hurts it by more. Airlines, cement, hotels and software products have high operating leverage, so their earnings and share prices are sensitive to volumes.
examples: With high operating leverage, a 10% sales rise lifted EBITDA 25%.
Hotels have huge operating leverage: occupancy up 5 points, profits up a third.
Operating leverage works both ways; in a slowdown, profits collapse.
terms.fill: A cement maker with mostly fixed costs sees profit jump 30% on a 10% rise in sales: that's ____.
wrong: Borrowing to fund expansion
Using futures to boost returns
Paying staff with shares

reads.up: When volumes rise for a high-operating-leverage company, margins expand fast and earnings upgrades follow; traders often buy early in the upcycle.
reads.down: When volumes fall, fixed costs crush margins; these stocks fall hardest at the start of a slowdown.

terms.short: Profit from outside the core business
terms.definition: Income that doesn't come from the main business: interest on cash, dividends, gains on investments or one-off sales. It can make profit look better than the business really is, so analysts strip it out to judge operating performance.
examples: PAT beat, but other income doubled; the core business missed.
Cash-rich IT firms earn a lot of other income from treasury.
Strip out other income and the profit growth is only 5%.
terms.fill: Interest earned on a company's cash pile is booked as ____.
wrong: Revenue from the main product
Money raised from issuing shares
Tax refunds from earlier years

reads.up: A jump in other income flatters profit but says little about the business; the market discounts beats that rely on it.
reads.down: Lower other income can make profit look weak even when operations are fine; read through to EBITDA.

terms.short: One-off gains or losses outside normal business
terms.definition: Unusual, non-recurring items such as a gain on selling a division, a big write-off, or a settlement. Companies report them separately so investors can see underlying profit. The market usually looks through them, unless they keep recurring.
examples: PAT fell because of a ₹300 crore exceptional item, an impairment; operations were fine.
Adjusted for exceptional items, profit grew 12%.
Exceptional items every quarter aren't exceptional any more.
terms.fill: A one-time ₹500 crore gain from selling a subsidiary is reported among the ____.
wrong: A gain from the main business
A dividend from a subsidiary
A rise in operating margin

terms.short: Cash the business generates from operations
terms.definition: The cash a company actually brings in from its business in a period, after paying suppliers, staff and taxes and after changes in working capital. Profit can be flattered by accounting; cash is harder to fake. Profit that never turns into operating cash flow is a warning sign.
examples: Profit rose 20%, but operating cash flow fell: receivables are piling up.
Operating cash flow covers capex comfortably, so they don't need to borrow.
The forensic analyst compares operating cash flow with EBITDA every year.
terms.fill: The cash a company brings in from running its business, after working capital changes, is its ____.
wrong: Cash raised by issuing shares
Cash spent on new factories
Cash on the balance sheet

reads.up: Rising operating cash flow backs up the profit story and funds growth without new debt; quality investors reward it.
reads.down: Falling operating cash flow while profit rises is a red flag: earnings may be stuck in receivables or inventory.

terms.short: Operating cash flow minus capex
terms.definition: Cash left after the business has paid for the investment it needs: operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. It can pay dividends, buy back shares or repay debt. Valuation models discount it, and steady free cash flow supports a higher multiple.
examples: Free cash flow turned positive as the capex cycle ended.
They pay dividends out of free cash flow, not borrowing.
A company with negative free cash flow every year keeps needing new money.
terms.fill: Operating cash flow of ₹800 crore minus ₹300 crore of capex leaves ₹500 crore of ____.
wrong: Profit after tax
Cash in the bank
Revenue minus costs

calcs.q: Operating cash flow is ₹1,200 crore and capex is ₹450 crore. What is free cash flow?
calcs.why: Free cash flow = operating cash flow − capex = 1,200 − 450 = ₹750 crore.

reads.up: Rising free cash flow means room for dividends, buybacks or paying down debt: usually a re-rating trigger.
reads.down: Falling or negative free cash flow means growth is being funded by debt or new shares; watch dilution and leverage.

terms.short: Money spent on long-term assets
terms.definition: Capital expenditure: spending on factories, machines, networks or other long-lived assets. Heavy capex now can mean growth later, but it uses cash and adds depreciation. Traders watch capex announcements for sectors such as cement, steel, power and the companies that supply them.
examples: The steelmaker announced ₹20,000 crore of capex, and capital goods stocks rallied.
Capex is peaking, so free cash flow should jump from next year.
Telecom capex for 5G weighed on cash flow for two years.
terms.fill: Spending ₹5,000 crore on a new plant is ____.
wrong: Spending on salaries and rent
Buying back the company's shares
Paying interest on debt

reads.up: A capex ramp-up signals expansion: good news for capital goods makers and suppliers; for the spender, the market asks whether returns will cover it.
reads.down: Falling capex can lift free cash flow in the short term, but a long freeze may mean weak demand or growth ahead.

terms.short: Cash tied up in stock and dues from customers
terms.definition: Current assets minus current liabilities: money stuck in inventory and receivables, less what the company owes suppliers. Growing businesses need more of it, which uses cash. A sudden jump can mean customers are paying late or stock isn't selling.
examples: Working capital rose by ₹400 crore as customers paid late, soaking up most of the year's cash.
FMCG companies run negative working capital: suppliers fund them.
Infrastructure firms often have heavy working capital tied up in government dues.
terms.fill: Inventory plus receivables, minus what's owed to suppliers, is the company's ____.
wrong: Its long-term borrowings
Its fixed assets
Cash raised in the IPO

reads.up: Working capital growing faster than sales is a warning: cash is stuck in unpaid bills or unsold stock.
reads.down: Shrinking working capital frees up cash; a falling cash cycle often lifts operating cash flow.

terms.short: How long customers take to pay
terms.definition: The average number of days a company waits to be paid: receivables ÷ sales × 365. Rising receivable days can mean customers are struggling or the company is pushing sales with easy credit. It is a common early sign of trouble in forensic accounting.
examples: Receivable days jumped from 60 to 95: are they booking sales they can't collect?
Government contractors have long receivable days.
Falling receivable days, as customers paid faster, helped cash flow beat profit.
terms.fill: Receivables of ₹250 crore on yearly sales of ₹1,000 crore mean about 91 ____.
wrong: Days of stock in the warehouse
Days to pay suppliers
Days until the next dividend

calcs.q: A company has receivables of ₹300 crore and annual sales of ₹1,825 crore. What are its receivable days?

reads.up: Rising receivable days suggests customers pay slower or sales are being stretched: a classic red flag for earnings quality.
reads.down: Falling receivable days means faster collection and better cash flow.

terms.short: How long stock sits before it's sold
terms.definition: The average days goods sit as inventory: inventory ÷ cost of goods sold × 365. A rise can mean demand is slowing or the company is stocking up ahead of price rises. In retail and autos, a build-up of dealer inventory often comes before discounts and weaker margins.
examples: Inventory days rose to 120; demand isn't keeping up with production.
Auto dealers are sitting on 50 inventory days, so expect festive discounts.
Lower inventory days, with goods selling faster, freed up ₹200 crore of cash.
terms.fill: Stock of ₹200 crore against yearly cost of goods of ₹1,200 crore is about 61 ____.
wrong: Days customers take to pay
Days of cash in the bank
Days to build a new factory

reads.up: Rising inventory days can mean demand is slowing: markdowns and margin pressure often follow.
reads.down: Falling inventory days usually means strong demand and healthy sell-through.

terms.short: Borrowing compared with shareholders' money
terms.definition: Total debt divided by shareholders' equity. It shows how much of the company is funded by lenders. High ratios amplify returns in good times and risk in bad times; lenders and the market penalise companies whose debt rises faster than earnings.
examples: Debt-to-equity is 2.5x, too high for a cyclical in a slowdown.
The rights issue cut debt-to-equity from 1.8 to 0.9.
Banks are judged on capital ratios, not debt-to-equity.
terms.fill: Debt of ₹3,000 crore against equity of ₹2,000 crore is a 1.5x ____.
wrong: Profit divided by sales
Share price divided by book value
Cash divided by short-term debt

reads.up: Rising debt-to-equity raises default risk and interest costs; stocks of heavily indebted firms fall hard when rates rise or growth slows.
reads.down: Falling debt-to-equity (deleveraging) lowers risk and often leads to a re-rating.

terms.short: How many times profit covers interest
terms.definition: Operating profit (EBIT) divided by interest expense. Below about 1.5x a company has little room for a bad quarter; above 5x interest is no worry. Lenders and rating agencies watch it closely.
examples: Interest coverage fell to 1.2x; one bad quarter and they can't pay.
With 8x interest coverage, the debt isn't the issue.
Rising rates cut interest coverage for floating-rate borrowers.
terms.fill: EBIT of ₹600 crore against interest of ₹150 crore gives 4x ____.
wrong: Dividends as a share of profit
Cash as a share of debt
Interest rate on the company's loans

calcs.q: EBIT is ₹480 crore and interest expense is ₹160 crore. What is interest coverage?
calcs.why: 480 ÷ 160 = 3: operating profit covers interest three times.

reads.up: Better interest coverage means debt is easier to service: less credit risk, and sometimes a rating upgrade.
reads.down: Falling interest coverage is an early sign of financial stress; credit spreads and the share price often react.

terms.short: Profit as a percentage of shareholders' equity
terms.definition: Return on equity: net profit divided by shareholders' equity. It shows how well the company earns on owners' money. High, steady ROE often supports a high price-to-book ratio. Debt can boost ROE, so read it with leverage.
examples: A 25% ROE for a decade is why the market pays 10x book for it.
ROE fell to 9% as the new plant sat idle.
Banks are often valued on ROE against price-to-book.
terms.fill: Net profit of ₹300 crore on equity of ₹1,500 crore is a 20% ____.
wrong: Profit as a share of sales
Dividend divided by price
Growth in net profit over a year

calcs.q: Net profit is ₹450 crore and shareholders' equity is ₹3,000 crore. What is ROE?

reads.up: Rising ROE usually means better profitability and supports a higher valuation; check it isn't only from more debt.
reads.down: Falling ROE suggests weaker returns on new money, and the stock often de-rates.

terms.short: Operating return on all capital, debt and equity
terms.definition: Return on capital employed: EBIT divided by capital employed (equity plus debt). Unlike ROE it isn't flattered by borrowing, so it is the better measure for comparing capital-heavy companies. A ROCE below the cost of capital destroys value as the company grows.
examples: ROCE of 30% means every new plant creates real value.
Debt pushed ROE up, but ROCE is stuck at 8%.
Investors in cement compare ROCE across companies, not ROE.
terms.fill: EBIT divided by equity plus debt is ____.
wrong: Profit as a share of sales
Dividends divided by equity
Share price divided by EPS

reads.up: Rising ROCE shows the business earns more on every rupee invested, a strong reason for a premium valuation.
reads.down: Falling ROCE means new investment is earning less; if it drops below the cost of capital, growth destroys value.

terms.short: Sales generated per rupee of assets
terms.definition: Revenue divided by total assets. Retailers and FMCG firms turn assets over fast; utilities and telecom slowly. With margin and leverage it is one of the three parts of ROE in the DuPont breakdown.
examples: The retailer's asset turnover is 3x, so even a 5% margin gives a good ROE.
Asset turnover fell because the new plant isn't running at capacity yet.
DuPont: ROE equals margin times asset turnover times leverage.
terms.fill: Sales of ₹4,000 crore on assets of ₹2,000 crore give an ____ of 2x.
wrong: Inventory divided by sales
Profit divided by assets
The share of assets that are fixed

reads.up: Higher asset turnover means assets are working harder: better ROE without needing better margins.
reads.down: Falling asset turnover often means idle capacity or slowing sales.

terms.short: How much profit turns into cash
terms.definition: Operating cash flow divided by EBITDA (or by net profit). A company converting 80% or more of EBITDA into cash is turning its profits into real money. Low or falling cash conversion suggests profits are stuck in working capital or aren't what they seem.
examples: Cash conversion of 95% says the profits are real.
Cash conversion fell to 40% as receivables ballooned.
The analyst prefers the company with lower growth but better cash conversion: its profit actually turns into cash.
terms.fill: Operating cash flow divided by EBITDA measures ____.
wrong: How fast inventory sells
How much profit is paid as dividends
How quickly debt is repaid

reads.up: Rising cash conversion shows profits turning into real cash: a sign of quality the market rewards.
reads.down: Weak cash conversion is a warning: profits may be stuck in working capital or flattered by accounting.

terms.short: How real and repeatable profit is
terms.definition: How much reported profit comes from the core business in cash, repeatedly, rather than from one-offs, aggressive accounting or unpaid bills. High-quality earnings deserve a higher multiple. Warning signs include profit far above cash flow, rising receivable days and frequent 'exceptional' items.
examples: Earnings quality is poor: profit is up but cash flow is negative for the third year.
The market pays up for earnings quality, which is why the FMCG stocks trade at 50x.
Frequent changes in accounting policy are a red flag for earnings quality.
terms.fill: Profit that is backed by cash and doesn't rely on one-offs shows high ____.
wrong: How much earnings grew this year
How close results came to estimates
Profit before tax and interest

terms.short: New shares cutting each holder's slice
terms.definition: When a company issues new shares, through a QIP, rights issue, stock options or a merger, each existing share owns a smaller part of the company, and EPS falls unless profit rises enough. Heavy, repeated dilution is a cost to shareholders even if the money raised is used well.
examples: The QIP means 8% dilution, so EPS estimates were cut.
Employee stock options cause steady dilution at tech companies.
The merger is 15% dilution for our shareholders.
terms.fill: Issuing 10% more shares, so each existing share owns less of the company, is ____.
wrong: A fall in the share price after results
Splitting each share into two
A company buying back its shares

reads.up: More dilution lowers EPS and often pressures the stock, unless the cash raised clearly earns more than it costs.
reads.down: Little or no dilution, or buybacks that shrink the share count, lift EPS for existing holders.

terms.short: P/E divided by expected earnings growth
terms.definition: The price-to-earnings ratio divided by the expected annual earnings growth rate in percent. A P/E of 40 with 40% growth gives a PEG of 1; the same P/E with 10% growth gives 4. It is a rough way to compare expensive-looking growth stocks.
examples: At a PEG ratio of 0.8 the stock isn't as expensive as its 40x P/E suggests.
A PEG ratio above 3 means you're paying a lot for the growth.
Growth forecasts are uncertain, and the PEG ratio divides the P/E by them, so treat it as a rough guide.
terms.fill: A P/E of 30 with expected earnings growth of 20% a year gives a ____ of 1.5.
wrong: Price divided by book value
Earnings growth over the last five years
Dividend divided by earnings

calcs.q: A stock trades at 45 times earnings, and earnings are expected to grow 15% a year. What is its PEG ratio?

terms.short: Enterprise value over operating profit
terms.definition: Enterprise value (market cap plus net debt) divided by EBITDA. Because it counts debt and ignores the capital structure, it compares companies with different borrowing better than P/E does, and is common in capital-heavy sectors like telecom, cement and metals.
examples: The cement deal valued the plant at 12x EV/EBITDA.
On EV/EBITDA, the debt-heavy telecom company isn't as cheap as its P/E suggests.
Metal stocks trade at 5x EV/EBITDA at the top of the cycle.
terms.fill: Market cap plus net debt, divided by operating profit, is the ____ multiple.
wrong: Price divided by earnings per share
Price divided by book value
Dividend divided by price

calcs.q: Market cap is ₹8,000 crore, net debt ₹2,000 crore and EBITDA ₹1,250 crore. What is EV/EBITDA?

terms.short: Value as today's worth of future cash flows
terms.definition: Discounted cash flow: a valuation that forecasts a company's free cash flows, discounts each back to today at the cost of capital, and adds a terminal value for the years beyond the forecast. The answer is very sensitive to the discount rate and the long-term growth assumed, so analysts show a range, not one number.
examples: Our DCF gives ₹1,450 a share, 20% above the market price.
Raise the discount rate by one point and the DCF value drops by 15%.
Most of the DCF value comes from the terminal value, so check the growth assumption first.
terms.fill: Forecasting free cash flows and discounting them back at the cost of capital is a ____ valuation.
wrong: Valuing a company at a multiple of peers' earnings
Valuing a company at the book value of its assets
Valuing a stock from its recent price trend

tf.s: In a typical DCF, most of the value comes from the first five forecast years.
tf.why: For a growing company the terminal value, covering everything after the forecast, is usually more than half of the total. That is why the long-term growth and discount rate matter so much.

terms.short: Blended cost of a company's debt and equity
terms.definition: Weighted average cost of capital: the return a company must earn to satisfy both its lenders and its shareholders, weighted by how much of each it uses. Debt is cheaper, and interest is tax-deductible, so it is counted after tax. A DCF discounts free cash flows at the WACC.
examples: The DCF uses a 12% WACC: 14% cost of equity, 8% post-tax cost of debt.
A project that earns less than the WACC destroys value, even if it is profitable.
Higher interest rates raised the WACC and cut our target price.
terms.fill: Cost of equity and post-tax cost of debt, weighted by how much of each is used, give the ____.
wrong: The interest rate on the company's latest loan
The return the company made on its equity last year
The dividend yield plus earnings growth
terms.formula: WACC = E/(D+E) × cost of equity + D/(D+E) × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate)

calcs.q: A company is 60% equity at a 15% cost of equity and 40% debt at 10% interest, with a 25% tax rate. What is its WACC?

terms.short: Value of all cash flows after the forecast
terms.definition: The value, at the end of a DCF's forecast period, of every cash flow after it. It is usually worked out by assuming cash flows grow at a steady rate forever (the Gordon growth formula) or by applying an exit multiple. It is often more than half of a DCF's answer, so a small change in long-term growth moves the value a lot.
examples: Terminal value is 70% of our DCF, so the 5% long-term growth assumption carries the whole call.
Using a 12x exit multiple instead of 5% perpetual growth gave a very different terminal value.
Long-term growth in the terminal value can't sensibly be above the economy's nominal growth.
terms.fill: In a DCF, the value of every cash flow after year ten is the ____.
wrong: The share price on the last day of the forecast
The book value of assets at the end of the forecast
The price the stock is expected to hit next year
terms.formula: Terminal value = FCF next year ÷ (WACC − g)

calcs.q: Free cash flow in the year after the forecast is ₹100 crore, WACC is 12% and long-term growth is 5%. What is the terminal value?
calcs.why: 100 ÷ (0.12 − 0.05) = 100 ÷ 0.07 ≈ ₹1,429 crore. That value is as of the end of the forecast, so it is then discounted back to today.

terms.short: The return shareholders require
terms.definition: The return shareholders expect for the risk of owning the stock. It isn't a bill the company pays, but a project that earns less is destroying their value. It is usually estimated with CAPM: the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium.
examples: With a 7% risk-free rate, 1.1 beta and 6% risk premium, the cost of equity is about 13.6%.
An ROE below the cost of equity means the stock should trade below book.
The bank's cost of equity is higher than its cost of deposits, so equity is its most expensive funding.
terms.fill: The return shareholders need for owning a risky stock, often estimated with CAPM, is the ____.
wrong: The interest rate the company pays on its loans
The dividend the company paid last year
The return the company actually earned on equity

tf.s: Equity is free money for a company, because unlike debt it has no interest to pay.
tf.why: Shareholders expect a return for their risk. Equity is usually more expensive than debt, because shareholders are paid last when things go wrong.

terms.short: Interest earned minus paid, over a bank's assets
terms.definition: Net interest income (interest earned minus interest paid) as a percentage of interest-earning assets. It is a bank's core profitability measure. It usually widens early in a rate-hiking cycle when loans reprice faster than deposits, and narrows when rates fall.
examples: Net interest margin fell 15 bps as deposit costs caught up.
Banks with more floating-rate loans saw a quick rise in net interest margin when the RBI hiked.
A 4% net interest margin is high for a large private bank.
terms.fill: Interest earned minus interest paid, as a share of earning assets, is a bank's ____.
wrong: The interest rate on fixed deposits
Profit after tax divided by equity
The share of loans that have gone bad

reads.up: Rising NIMs mean higher core profits for banks: bank stocks usually react well.
reads.down: Compressing NIMs squeeze bank earnings; the market often de-rates lenders when NIM guidance is cut.

terms.short: Bad loans as a share of all loans
terms.definition: Non-performing assets: loans where interest or principal is overdue for more than 90 days, as a percentage of total loans, before provisions. Net NPA subtracts provisions. Rising NPAs mean more provisions and lower profits ahead.
examples: Gross NPA rose to 4.2% from 3.6%, mostly from unsecured retail loans.
The PSU bank rally of the last few years came as gross NPA fell steadily.
Watch slippages: they tell you where gross NPA is heading.
terms.fill: Loans overdue by more than 90 days, as a share of all loans, give a bank's ____ ratio.
wrong: A bank's profit as a share of its loans
Deposits as a share of loans
Loans given to priority sectors

reads.up: Rising gross NPAs mean more provisions and weaker profits; bank stocks usually sell off on asset-quality worries.
reads.down: Falling NPAs mean cleaner books and lower provisions ahead: a common trigger for re-rating.

terms.short: Share of deposits in low-cost accounts
terms.definition: The share of a bank's deposits in current and savings accounts, which pay little or no interest, against higher-cost fixed deposits. A high CASA ratio means cheaper funding and better margins. When rates rise, savers move to fixed deposits and the ratio usually falls.
examples: The CASA ratio slipped from 45% to 40% as customers moved to FDs.
A high CASA ratio is why the big private bank can lend cheaper.
Falling CASA ratio is pushing up deposit costs across the sector.
terms.fill: Current and savings deposits as a share of all deposits is the bank's ____.
wrong: The share of loans in cash
Capital as a share of risk assets
Cash reserves held with the RBI

reads.up: A rising CASA ratio lowers funding costs and supports margins: positive for the bank.
reads.down: A falling CASA ratio raises funding costs and squeezes NIM.

terms.short: Average revenue per user
terms.definition: Average revenue per user per month, the key number for telecom, and also used by internet and media companies. Tariff hikes and customers moving to costlier plans lift it. Analysts model telecom earnings mostly from subscribers × ARPU.
examples: ARPU rose to ₹200 after the tariff hike, and the stock hit a record.
Subscriber growth is slowing, so ARPU has to do the work.
Every ₹10 of ARPU adds thousands of crores to telecom EBITDA.
terms.fill: Total monthly revenue divided by the number of subscribers is the telecom firm's ____.
wrong: The cost of adding a new customer
The share of customers who leave each month
Revenue from enterprise clients

reads.up: Rising ARPU, usually from tariff hikes, drops almost straight to EBITDA for telecoms: very positive for the stocks.
reads.down: Falling ARPU means price competition or customers trading down; earnings estimates get cut.

terms.short: Sales growth from stores open over a year
terms.definition: Growth in sales at stores that were open in both periods, leaving out new openings. It shows whether existing stores are really selling more. Retail, quick-service restaurant and jewellery stocks react strongly to it.
examples: Same-store sales growth of 2% while total sales grew 20%: growth is only from new stores.
The QSR chain's same-store sales growth turned negative, and the stock fell 8%.
Investors watch same-store sales growth to see if demand is real.
terms.fill: Sales growth at outlets open for more than a year, excluding new stores, is ____.
wrong: Total sales growth including new stores
Growth in the number of stores
Online sales as a share of total

reads.up: Strong same-store sales growth shows healthy underlying demand and pricing: retail stocks usually rerate on it.
reads.down: Weak or negative SSSG means existing stores are struggling, even if new openings lift total sales.

terms.short: Orders won but not yet delivered
terms.definition: The value of contracts a company has won but not yet executed, important for capital goods, defence, infrastructure and engineering firms. A backlog several times annual revenue gives visibility of future sales. Order inflow, the new orders won in a period, shows where it is heading.
examples: The order backlog is ₹4 lakh crore, about four years of revenue.
Defence stocks rallied on record order inflow, swelling the order backlog.
A big backlog is only good if they can execute it on time and on margin.
terms.fill: Contracts won but not yet carried out, giving years of revenue visibility, form the ____.
wrong: The queue of buy orders at the exchange
Unpaid bills from customers
Unsold stock in the warehouse

reads.up: A growing backlog and strong order inflow mean visible future revenue: capital goods and defence stocks often rally on it.
reads.down: A shrinking backlog warns of slower revenue ahead; the stocks often fall before the sales do.

terms.short: Share of staff who leave in a year
terms.definition: The percentage of employees who leave over a year, closely watched for IT services firms, where people are the main cost. High attrition raises hiring and wage costs and squeezes margins; falling attrition usually helps margins.
examples: Attrition rate hit 25% during the hiring boom, and margins took a hit.
Falling attrition rate gives the IT firm room to expand margins.
Investors ask about attrition rate on every IT earnings call.
terms.fill: An IT firm losing 18 of every 100 employees over a year has an 18% ____.
wrong: Growth in the number of clients
The share of revenue from the US
Revenue per employee

reads.up: Rising attrition pushes up wage and hiring costs; IT margins and stocks usually suffer.
reads.down: Falling attrition eases cost pressure and supports IT margins.

terms.short: Value of new IT deals won
terms.definition: The total value of new deals an IT services firm signs in a quarter, over their whole life. It is the leading indicator for future revenue growth, so a strong TCV can lift a stock even when the current quarter is weak.
examples: Total contract value of $2 billion this quarter points to faster growth next year.
Revenue missed, but record total contract value sent the stock up.
Large deals with long ramp-ups take time to turn TCV into revenue.
terms.fill: An IT firm signing $1.5 billion of new multi-year deals in a quarter reports that as its ____.
wrong: Revenue booked this quarter
Market value of the company
Value of shares bought back

reads.up: Strong TCV signals revenue growth ahead; IT stocks often rally on large deal wins even with a soft quarter.
reads.down: Weak TCV warns of slower growth in coming quarters; analysts cut estimates.

terms.short: Group numbers including subsidiaries
terms.definition: Results that add up the parent company and all its subsidiaries, as one group. Indian companies also file standalone results for the parent alone. Traders read consolidated numbers for most groups, because a strong parent can hide a loss-making subsidiary, and the reverse.
examples: Standalone profit rose 20%, but consolidated results fell because the overseas arm lost money.
Always check whether the street's estimate is on consolidated or standalone numbers.
The holding company looks cheap on standalone, but consolidated results show the debt.
terms.fill: Numbers that add the parent and all its subsidiaries together are the ____.
wrong: Results of the parent company alone
Results for the full year only
Results restated after an audit

terms.short: Slides a company releases with results
terms.definition: A slide deck filed on the exchange with or just after results. It gives the KPIs the filing leaves out: volumes, segment splits, order book, store counts, client numbers. Read it before the earnings call, because the call's questions usually start from it.
examples: The investor presentation showed volumes up 12%, which the press release didn't mention.
Compare this quarter's investor presentation with last year's; a dropped KPI slide is a hint.
The bank's investor presentation has the slippage and restructured book numbers.
terms.fill: The slide deck a company files with its results, full of KPIs, is the ____.
wrong: The auditor's report on the accounts
A broker's research note on the stock
The notice for the AGM

terms.short: What the bosses say about the outlook
terms.definition: What the CEO and CFO say about demand, margins, costs and plans, in the press release and on the earnings call. Markets often move more on the tone of the commentary than on the quarter's numbers, because it is about the next quarters, not the last one.
examples: Results missed, but management commentary on demand was upbeat and the stock rose.
Management commentary turned cautious on rural demand for the first time in a year.
Track the commentary across calls; promises that keep slipping are a warning.
terms.fill: The CEO's remarks on the call that rural demand still feels cautious are ____.
wrong: The auditor's opinion on the accounts
A broker's change in rating
The board's dividend decision

reads.up: A more confident tone, with clear numbers behind it, can lift the stock even on a weak quarter and leads analysts to raise estimates.
reads.down: A more cautious tone, or vaguer answers than last time, often hits the stock harder than a miss, because it points to downgrades ahead.

terms.short: Revenue and profit by business line
terms.definition: The breakdown of revenue, profit and capital employed by each business or region, which listed companies must give with results. It shows which part is growing, which is losing money, and where the group's profit really comes from.
examples: Segment results showed retail growing 30% while the legacy business shrank.
Two-thirds of profit came from one segment, so the stock trades on that business.
The new segment is still losing money; watch whether its losses narrow.
terms.fill: A table of revenue and profit for each business line of a company shows its ____.
wrong: Profit by quarter for the last five years
Shareholding by investor type
Costs by type of expense

reads.up: A rising share of profit from the fast-growing or high-margin segment usually earns the whole group a higher multiple.
reads.down: A shrinking or loss-making segment drags the group; the market cheers if the company sells or shuts it, and worries if it keeps funding it.

terms.short: Who owns the shares, filed quarterly
terms.definition: The quarterly filing that shows what share of a company is held by promoters, FIIs, mutual funds and other domestic institutions, and retail. It comes out within 21 days of the quarter end. Changes from quarter to quarter show who is buying and who is selling.
examples: The shareholding pattern showed mutual funds raised their stake from 6% to 9%.
Promoters cut their holding again; check the shareholding pattern for pledges too.
FII holding fell for four quarters in a row while retail holding rose.
terms.fill: The quarterly filing that splits ownership between promoters, FIIs, DIIs and retail is the ____.
wrong: The list of the board's directors
The register of bondholders
The list of the top clients

reads.up: Rising promoter or institutional holding signals confidence from people who know the stock well and is usually read as positive.
reads.down: Falling promoter holding, or steady FII and mutual fund selling, is read as insiders and big money stepping back; check why.

terms.short: How far results land from the estimate
terms.definition: The gap between reported numbers and the consensus estimate, usually as a percentage. The stock reacts to the surprise, not to the growth: 20% growth is bad news if the street expected 30%. Big surprises are often followed by further drift in the same direction.
examples: Profit grew 40%, but the street expected 50%, so the earnings surprise was negative.
The earnings surprise was +12%, the biggest in the sector this season.
After a big positive earnings surprise, the stock kept drifting up for weeks.
terms.fill: Profit 10% above the consensus estimate is a positive ____.
wrong: The change in the share price on results day
Growth against the same quarter last year
A one-off gain in the profit and loss

reads.up: A positive surprise, especially on revenue and margins, usually lifts the stock and leads to estimate upgrades over the next weeks.
reads.down: A negative surprise usually sends the stock down even if growth looks fine, and the selling can last as analysts cut estimates.

terms.short: New orders won in the quarter
terms.definition: The value of new contracts a company won in the period, used for capital goods, defence, infrastructure and IT services companies. Revenue tells you about the past; order inflow tells you about revenue in the coming years. Compare it with revenue: inflow above revenue grows the order book.
examples: Order inflow of ₹20,000 crore was twice the quarter's revenue, so the backlog grew.
Weak order inflow worried the market more than the earnings beat.
Defence stocks rallied on record order inflow from the ministry.
terms.fill: The value of new contracts a company signed this quarter is its ____.
wrong: Orders still to be executed
Revenue billed in the quarter
Cash collected from customers

reads.up: Strong order inflow, especially above revenue, points to faster revenue growth ahead and usually supports a higher multiple.
reads.down: Slowing inflow means the order book will shrink and growth will slow in a year or two; the stock often falls before the revenue does.

terms.short: The full yearly report with audited accounts
terms.definition: The yearly document every listed company publishes: audited financial statements, notes to accounts, the auditor's report, management discussion, governance, related party dealings and pay. The quarterly filings are short; the annual report is where the detail and the problems are.
examples: The annual report showed a large loan to a promoter company that the quarterly results never mentioned.
Read the annual report before the AGM; questions get better answers there.
Analysts compare five years of annual reports to see how the story has changed.
terms.fill: The yearly document with audited accounts, the auditor's report and management discussion is the ____.
wrong: A quarter's results filing
A broker's initiation report
The company's offer document for an IPO

terms.short: Management's own review of the year
terms.definition: Management Discussion and Analysis: the section of the annual report where the company explains its industry, its performance, risks and outlook in words. It is where management sets expectations and where you can check whether last year's promises were kept.
examples: Last year's MD&A promised 15% growth; actual growth was 6%.
The MD&A flagged rising competition for the first time.
Read the MD&A for the risks section; it often warns before the numbers do.
terms.fill: The annual report section where management explains performance, risks and outlook is the ____.
wrong: The auditor's opinion on the accounts
The board's remuneration table
The cash flow statement

terms.short: The fine print under the financials
terms.definition: The pages after the financial statements that explain the numbers: accounting policies, debt terms, loans given, tax disputes, one-offs and guarantees. Most red flags in Indian companies have been in the notes long before they hit the headline numbers.
examples: The notes to accounts showed the company changed its depreciation policy to lift profit.
A large loan to an unnamed party sat in the notes to accounts.
Read the notes to accounts on borrowings: the covenants are there.
terms.fill: The pages after the financial statements explaining policies, debt terms and disputes are the ____.
wrong: The chairman's letter to shareholders
The investor presentation
The list of subsidiaries

terms.short: Deals with promoters' own entities
terms.definition: Business the company does with entities linked to its promoters, directors or group firms: buying, selling, renting, lending or paying royalties. They are allowed with approvals, but they are the easiest way to move money out of a listed company, so investors watch their size and trend.
examples: Related party transactions were 30% of sales, all with promoter-owned distributors.
Shareholders voted down the royalty increase to the parent, a related party transaction.
The company lent ₹500 crore to a group firm, flagged under related party transactions.
terms.fill: Sales to a distributor owned by the promoter's family are ____.
wrong: Trades by insiders in the company's shares
Deals between two unrelated listed firms
Payments to the company's auditors

reads.up: Rising related party dealings, especially loans or payments to promoter firms, are a governance red flag and usually cut the multiple the market pays.
reads.down: Falling related party dealings, or a merger that folds them in, is read as cleaner governance and can lead to a re-rating.

terms.short: Possible costs not on the balance sheet
terms.definition: Obligations that may become real depending on an event: tax disputes, legal claims, guarantees given for other companies' loans. They sit in the notes, not in the balance sheet. A large figure compared with net worth means one bad ruling could wipe out years of profit.
examples: Contingent liabilities from tax disputes were 60% of net worth.
The company had guaranteed a group firm's loan, so it sat in contingent liabilities: nothing is owed unless that firm defaults.
The stock fell when a court ruling turned a contingent liability into a real one.
terms.fill: A pending tax demand the company is fighting in court is one of its ____.
wrong: Loans already on the balance sheet
Profits not yet booked
Unpaid dividends to shareholders

reads.up: Growing contingent liabilities, especially guarantees for group firms, raise the risk of a sudden hit to net worth; the market discounts the stock for it.
reads.down: Falling contingent liabilities, as disputes are settled or guarantees released, remove an overhang and can lift the stock.

terms.short: The auditor won't fully sign off
terms.definition: An auditor's report that says the accounts are fair except for specific matters it could not verify or disagrees with. It is more serious than an 'emphasis of matter', which only draws attention to something. A qualification on cash, receivables or related parties is a major warning.
examples: The auditor gave a qualified audit opinion on ₹800 crore of receivables it couldn't verify.
The stock fell 15% after the auditors would not fully sign off on receivables, issuing their qualified audit opinion.
Read the auditor's report first; a qualified audit opinion changes everything else.
terms.fill: An auditor saying the accounts are fair 'except for' a matter it couldn't verify is a ____.
wrong: A clean report with no comments
The board's approval of the results
A rating agency's downgrade

terms.short: Auditors quitting mid-term: a red flag
terms.definition: When the statutory auditor resigns before finishing its term. Companies must file the reason with the exchange. Reasons like 'information not provided' have come before many Indian accounting scandals, so the market treats a mid-term exit as a serious warning.
examples: The auditor resigned citing lack of information, and the stock hit the lower circuit.
Two auditor resignations in three years: most funds won't touch the stock.
Check the resignation letter filed with the exchange, not just the company's statement.
terms.fill: The statutory auditor quitting mid-term citing 'information not provided' is an ____.
wrong: A director leaving the board
A change of the company's registrar
The CFO retiring on schedule

terms.short: Revenue, costs and profit over a period
terms.definition: The statement that shows what a company earned and spent over a quarter or a year: revenue at the top, then costs, interest, depreciation and tax, down to net profit at the bottom. Indian filings call it the statement of profit and loss. It shows profit, not cash: a sale on credit counts here before any money arrives.
examples: The income statement showed record profit, but the cash flow statement showed receivables piling up.
Start at the top of the income statement: did revenue grow, or only margins?
Other income was 40% of profit before tax on the income statement this quarter.
terms.fill: Revenue at the top, net profit at the bottom, for one quarter: that's the ____.
wrong: A snapshot of what the company owns and owes on one date
The cash that came in and went out over the year
A list of the company's shareholders

tf.s: A company can report a profit on its income statement and still run out of cash.
tf.why: Profit counts sales when they are made, not when they are paid for. If customers pay late or stock builds up, cash can drain while profit looks fine.

terms.short: What a company owns and owes, on one date
terms.definition: A snapshot on one date, usually the end of a quarter or year: assets on one side, and on the other the liabilities owed to lenders and suppliers plus the shareholders' equity. The two sides always balance, because everything the company owns was paid for with either borrowed money or owners' money.
examples: The balance sheet shows ₹2,000 crore of debt against ₹1,500 crore of equity.
Listed Indian companies publish the balance sheet every half year, not every quarter.
Net cash on the balance sheet covers the whole market cap of the subsidiary.
terms.fill: Assets on one side, liabilities plus shareholders' equity on the other, as of 31 March: the ____.
wrong: Revenue and costs over a full year
The cash received and paid during the quarter
The company's plan for next year's spending

tf.s: A balance sheet shows how much profit the company made during the year.
tf.why: The balance sheet is a snapshot of what is owned and owed on one date. Profit over a period is on the income statement.

terms.short: Where the cash came from and went
terms.definition: The statement of actual cash in and out over a period, split three ways: operating (running the business), investing (capex, buying or selling businesses) and financing (borrowing, repaying, dividends, buybacks). It is the hardest statement to dress up, so analysts check it against reported profit.
examples: Operating cash flow on the cash flow statement was half of net profit, which worried the analyst.
The cash flow statement shows the dividend was paid out of new borrowing.
Investing outflows jumped on the cash flow statement because of the new plant.
terms.fill: Cash from operations, from investing and from financing are the three parts of the ____.
wrong: Revenue and costs over the year
What the company owns and owes on one date
Forecasts of next year's earnings

tf.s: Paying a dividend shows up in the investing section of the cash flow statement.
tf.why: Dividends, borrowing, repayments and buybacks are financing cash flows. Investing covers capex and buying or selling businesses and investments.

terms.short: Revenue left after the direct cost of goods
terms.definition: Revenue minus the direct cost of making or buying what was sold (raw materials, goods bought for resale), as a share of revenue. It shows pricing power and input costs before rent, salaries and other overheads. For a paint or FMCG company, raw-material prices move it every quarter.
examples: Crude fell, so the paint maker's gross margin expanded by 300 basis points.
Gross margin held up, so the profit drop came from higher ad spend, not costs of goods.
A retailer's gross margin is thin, so it lives on volume.
terms.fill: Revenue minus raw-material cost, divided by revenue, is the ____.
wrong: Profit after every cost, interest and tax
Money blocked by a broker to hold a position
The gap between the bid and the ask
terms.formula: Gross margin = (Revenue − Cost of goods sold) ÷ Revenue

calcs.q: Revenue is ₹500 crore and the cost of goods sold is ₹300 crore. What is the gross margin?

reads.up: A wider gross margin usually means lower input costs or stronger pricing, and often lifts earnings estimates for the next quarters.
reads.down: A narrower gross margin points to rising input costs or price cuts; analysts check whether the company can pass the costs on.

terms.short: Operating profit (EBIT) as a share of revenue
terms.definition: Operating profit, or EBIT (earnings before interest and tax), divided by revenue. Unlike EBITDA margin it is after depreciation, so it counts the cost of wearing out plants and equipment. It shows how much of each rupee of sales the core business keeps before financing costs and tax.
examples: Operating margin fell even though EBITDA margin rose, because depreciation on the new plant kicked in.
IT services firms guide on operating margin, usually in a band like 20–22%.
An operating margin of 8% leaves little room if wages rise.
terms.fill: EBIT divided by revenue, after depreciation but before interest and tax, is the ____.
wrong: Profit before depreciation, as a share of revenue
Net profit as a share of shareholders' equity
Revenue left after raw materials only

calcs.q: Revenue is ₹1,000 crore, EBITDA is ₹200 crore and depreciation is ₹50 crore. What is the operating margin?
calcs.why: EBIT = EBITDA − depreciation = 200 − 50 = 150. Operating margin = 150 ÷ 1,000 = 15%. The EBITDA margin is 20%.

reads.up: A rising operating margin means the core business is keeping more of each rupee of sales; it usually drives earnings upgrades.
reads.down: A falling operating margin, from wages, costs or price cuts, usually leads to earnings downgrades even if revenue grows.

terms.short: Short-term assets over short-term debts
terms.definition: Current assets (cash, receivables, inventory, anything turning into cash within a year) divided by current liabilities (what must be paid within a year). Above 1 means the company can cover its near-term bills from near-term assets. Too low is a liquidity worry; very high can mean cash or stock sitting idle.
examples: A current ratio of 0.8 means short-term bills exceed short-term assets.
The lender's covenant requires a current ratio above 1.2.
Inventory is most of the current assets, so the current ratio flatters the real liquidity.
terms.fill: Current assets divided by current liabilities is the ____.
wrong: Debt divided by shareholders' equity
Operating profit divided by interest cost
Share price divided by earnings per share
terms.formula: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities

calcs.q: Current assets are ₹600 crore and current liabilities are ₹400 crore. What is the current ratio?
calcs.why: 600 ÷ 400 = 1.5: near-term assets cover near-term bills one and a half times.

terms.short: Share of profit paid out as dividends
terms.definition: Dividends paid divided by net profit. A high payout suits mature, cash-rich companies such as PSUs and FMCG firms; a low one means profit is kept to fund growth. A payout above 100% means the dividend is coming out of past savings or borrowing, which can't last.
examples: The PSU's dividend payout ratio is 60%, so most of the profit comes back to shareholders.
A payout above 100% this year was funded from reserves.
Growth companies keep the dividend payout ratio low and reinvest.
terms.fill: Dividends of ₹40 out of a net profit of ₹100 mean a ____ of 40%.
wrong: Dividend per share divided by the share price
The date you must hold shares to get a dividend
Profit kept in the business each year

calcs.q: A company earns ₹50 per share and pays ₹20 per share in dividends. What is its payout ratio?
calcs.why: 20 ÷ 50 = 40% of profit paid out; the other 60% is kept in the business.

tf.s: A high dividend payout ratio and a high dividend yield are the same thing.
tf.why: Payout compares dividends with profit. Yield compares dividends with the share price. A stock can pay out most of its profit and still yield little if the price is high.
